I do not want to hint that the Montreal ' Star ' had anything to do with this, because every one knows that the Montreal ' Star ' is an independent journal. I do not know that any one can say where they came from or who sent them or who supplied the money so lavishly. They may have come of their own accord and may have been using their own money for anything I know.
After all the abuse that has been heapetd on our devoted heads by the Conservative papers during the last three months about this; Guysborough election and about the part taken in it by Dominion officials, it seems to have come down to one ease. I take very little account of the names read here, by hon. gentlemen opposite. They have secured the names of certain men in the public service in Guysborough and have said that they were told by some one that these men took an active part in the election. I do not know that they took an active part. Some gentlemen in discussing this question wanted me to deny that they did. I am not aware that those gentlemen did take an active part and there is not the slightest proof that they did. It appears that it comes down to the name of one man, a Mr. LeBlanc, and that they have secured some evidence that that man took some part in that election. They scoured Guysborough from end to end, for evidence in respect to this matter and we are told by the Truro ' Sun ' an organ of the Conservative party in Nova Scotia that a representative of the Montreal ' Star ' came to the province for that special purpose and spent about a week in the province looking up information, and yet they have only been able to discover one man against whom they can make a definite charge. Counting all thb Dominon officials there, postmasters, and fishery officers and custom house officers and railway employees, I suppose there are between two hundred and three hundred men in that constituency alone, and if they are only able to find one who has actually overstepped the bounds and done something that he should not have done in this election, I think that is not a very bad showing for the Liberal party. In the case of this solitary official I am told that he

was not then in the employ of the Intercolonial Railway ; that he obtained three months leave of absence owing to some accident that had happened to him and was not fitted for work. It was during his vacation that he took his little trip down to Guysborough. I am informed that is a fact and I believe it to be true. Do you imagine, if the position was reversed and lion, gentlemen opposite were in power, that we would only have to complain of the interference of one official in Guysborough ? Under the system that prevailed prior to 1890 nearly every single official was an election agent of the Conservative party and they were expected to be election agents. The bounty cheques, for example, were used as a sort' of campaign fund in Guysborough in those days and I am informed that the time for the distribution of these cheques was arranged so that they were handed out to the fishermen at the time that the Conservative candidate was making his canvass along the shore. Another scheme was to levy tines against the fishermen for political purposes, fines that were never attempted to be collected. A fisherman was selected and was charged with having small lobsters in his possession or some such offence and a fine of $15 or $20 was entered against him but no attempt was made to collect the fine. Then, when an election came on, we would have a list of the names of these fishermen along the shore of that county-and I believe of every county in Nova Scotia-that were popularly known as lobster votes. We used to mark opposite them that they were lobster votes and we could not expect to get any of them to support the Liberal party. The heelers of the Conservative party came to these men and said : If y'ou vote for the Conservative candidate, this fine will not be collected ; but if you vote for the Liberal candidate, a distress warrant will be issued to-morrow morning. In this way they used to hold the fines over these people and secure their votes from election to election. These were some of the methods adopted by hou., gentlemen opposite when in power. That was only eight short years ago, but since they have got into opposition they have grown very pure and go into hysterics over the case of one official who took an active part in an election.

Hon. gentlemen opposite take the ground that no man who is an official of the government should have anything to do with an election, but they surely do not forget that when they were in office we had some
200 revising barristers, many of whom were active and offensive partisans. They were the men who made the lists and decided who should and who should not vote. The discussion we are having to-day seems to have been deliberately planned by our hon. friends opposite. It is nearly two months since the Truro ' Sun ' made the following announcement :-
During the recent by-election in Guysborough, Mr. B. A. Macnab, a Montreal newspaper man, well known in the commercial metropolis, journeyed to New Glasgow. There he remained a week. His presence in that place drew from the local Grit paper a perfect tirade of abuse. The visitor was accused of being a corruptionist ; he was styled a second edition of ' Cap.' Sullivan. A more flagrant series of prima facie libels could not well be conceived.
Mr. Mcnab made no sign. He left New Glasgow when his work was over. What that "work was is now becoming apparent. The revelations of corrupt methods employed in the Guysborough campaign are alleged to be due to his initiative. It would appear that during the campaign he had arranged a plan to bring to light the devious methods of the Liberals. And now, day 'by day, some new phase of crooked work is being brought out. The climax will, it is said, he reached when the matter is brought up in the House of Commons in connection with the passage of salaries,, in the estimates, of some of the government employees who took an active part in the fight. The affidavits in these particular cases are said to be very interesting.
We did have .one affidavit mentioned by tbe hon. member for Pictou, but I do not think he told us the name of the man who made it, nor did he give us the whole affidavit. He read some remarks from a paper which he said was an affidavit, and said that Mr. LeBlanc had taken an active part iu this election. The Truro ' Sun ' is one of the leading organs of the Conservative party in Nova Scotia. The editor of that paper is said to be high up in the ranks of that party and ought to know what he^ is talking about. He tells us that Mr. McNab came to Glasgow and remained there a week without making any sign. He is evidently a mysterious character is Mr. McNab. He was to old a campaigner to make any sign by which his real mission to Nova Scotia might be understood. The 1 Sun ' goes on to say that he was the author of all these revelations which we have been having in the Conservative papers with regard to that county. In other words, that he was the instigator of all these slanders and falsehoods scattered throughout Canada in the Conservative press regarding the people of Guysborough. The statements of the ' Sun ' may or may not be true, but l have it on good evidence that the room which this hon. gentleman occupied fit the Norfolk House at New Glasgow seemed to be tbe Iheadquarters of tbe Conservative 'party and was tbe place where the Conservative agents and heelers got their instructions before starting out on their various routes for the county of Guysborough. I am not

charging Mr. McNab with having done anything out of the way because personally I have no knowledge and have no charge to make against him. He may have been distributing religious tracts or prayer books, for aught I know.

speechtext: But I find the explanation of the 'Sun ' rather peculiar that he remained there a whole week getting up imaginary revelations, and revelations which were not given to the public for something like six weeks after the election was over and therefore could have no part in the result. That, however, was the explanation given by the 'Sun. ' We were told that the climax would be reached when this matter would be brought up hi the House of Commons. I suppose it is the climax we are having to-day. There is certainly a great deal of noise over a very small matter, but that is becoming characteristic of hon. gentlemen opposite. To quote the language indulged in by the great D. V. Johnson's ghost in the ' Rejected Addresses,' it is not the first time this session, Mr. Speaker, that the parturient mountain to your left has been in labour and has brought forth a mus-cipular abortion. These hon. gentlemen opposite attacked the Prime Minister over the non-production of the memorandum of the Grand Trunk Pacific and later on attacked the Minister of Railways because he would not make a speech, but when he did, there was not a single man on that side who undertook to answer it. Their recent attack on the Minister of Agriculture also was another evidence of a great deal of ado about nothing, and to-day it seems we are reaching the climax. I do not wish to be understood as advocating a policy of employing Dominion officials to do campaign work, but when one is discovered doing work of this kind, he ought to have the sympathy of hon. gentlemen opposite. They themselves furnished us with an illustrious example in the ease of Sir Charles Tupper. It will be remembered that in 1891 or 1892, when Sir Charles Tup-uer, Bart., was High Commissioner of Canada, drawing a large salary from the people, he came across the Atlantic, and while his salary was still running, stumped Nova Scotia in the interests of the Conservative party. The Liberals in this House then protested. They said it was not fan' that a man at the very head of the civil service, drawing a very large salary, should be allowed to conduct himself in that way, but I have yet to hear that any hon. gentleman opposite ever protested against his conduct.

I think that ought to clear up the record with regard to Mr. Kirk. He went to St. Mary's, his old home ; he went there for the purpose of voting for the Liberal candidate -I have no doubt that that is what he went for-he deposited his ballot and no more. He did not canvass any of the electors, or attempt to influence the vote of any elector, or. take any part in the election. Why should his name be bandied about in the newspapers or hints be thrown out on the floor of this House that he had done something that he should not have done ? I feel that hon. members should exonerate Mr. Kirk, and I believe that such statements will not be repeated, because, X have not the slightest doubt that every word that Mr. Kirk has written in regard to this incident is true.
I was a little surprised that the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) should make reference to corrupt practices on the part of the Liberal party in the Guysborough election. I do not know that it is a good thing to wash our dirty linen here, but, if the hon. gentleman wants to discuss the question of corruption in connection with the Guysborough election, I am quite ready. I have been asked by hon. gentlemen on the other side to discuss this question of corrupt practices in the Guysborough election, That is my excuse for trespassing any longer on the time of the House. A great many charges have been made in the public press regarding corrupt practices by the Liberals, but I notice that there is an utter absence of detail. Our opponents have had an opportunity to protest that election, but they let that opportunity go by. It was an election that certainly aroused a great deal of interest in the eastern part of Nova Scotia, as well as in other parts of Canada, and, if there was anything done by the Liberal party on that occasion that they ought not to have done there is not the slightest doubt they would have taken the occasion to protest that election. On that occasion I had the assistance for a few days of Mr. E. M. MacDonald, M.P.P., of Pictou. I do not need to tell hon. members of this House who Mr. MacDonald is. He is one of the rising young men of Nova Scotia, and i am looking forward to the time after the next general election when he will take his seat in this House as a supporter of the government and representative of the once Conservative but now Liberal county of Pictou. I asked Mr. MacDonald, who was present at one of the polling booths at that election to give me a statement of the facts that came under his personal knowledge. I was aware that certain things were done in the polling booth at which I was, as I have already told the committee, and was aware that similar things were being done in other polling booths in the county. Mr. MacDonald wrote :
With reference to matters in Guysborough, I beg to state to you some things that occurred during my stay in the county. I may say I arrived there the evening before nomination day and spoke in Guysborough nomination night, in Port Mulgrave on Thursday night, and returned to Guysborough with Pre-

mier Murray on Friday afternoon. I left Guysborough on Saturday with the premier and drove to Canso, spoke there that night, and Monday morning I drove to Port Felix where I addressed a meeting that night, and on Tuesday afternoon I spoke at Charlos Cove, and Tuesday evening at Larry's River, remaining there until election evening when I drove to Guysborough. On nomination day there appeared at Guysborough a man whom I afterwards discovered to be Mr. Prieur, of Montreal, who was closeted that evening in Grant's Hotel with Messrs. Chas. E. Tanner and E. C. Gregory.

Tanner is the deader of the Conservative party in the local legislature of Nova Scotia ; he is the Conservative organizer in that province and the leader of such opposition as we have there :
On arriving at Charlos Cove I found that he had been there at the house of Charles Richard since the previous Thursday and that he was accompanied by a man whom the people in that locality called ' Twlger,' which was evidently an assumed name. I found that he had not had any meetings but had been sending for people in that vicinity and interviewing them privately during the week he had been there, and that his conduct had been exceedingly mysterious and wholly different from that of a man who was looking for votes on the ground of principle. On Tuesday afternoon I called at the house where he was but he declined to see me In response to a message I sent to his room inviting him to come to my meeting, the answer was that he was no speaker and did not take any part in meetings. The next day he appeared at Larry's River poll and had his headquarters in the house of a man named Michael Pelrine. His companion ' Twiger ' appeared as the agent of Giffin under the name of ' Switzer.' Giffin, the Conservative candidate, was also in and about the house during the day, and from which drunken men emanated throughout the day. That Prieur was not engaged in discussing politics with the electors was evident, and one man, William Petipas, told me he had received money from him to vote for Giffin and that he had taken an oath to vote that way. Before leaving Port Felix on Tuesday morning i discovered that two men whose names were not known, and who I think did not belong to Nova Scotia, were there working in the interests of the Conservative party. In addition to these two men and Prieur and Switzer, the following men were in the county who did not address meetings :-John Baillie, Pictou ; H. V. Jen-nison, New Glasgow ; Mr. Simson, Halifax, who worked in Queensport district ; Mr. Parsons, Halifax ; Joseph A. Gillies, Sydney. Tanner spoke at only one meeting while he was there for a week, and other persons whose names I do not know.
Now, Sir, on that occasion in addition to the parties named by Mr. MacDonald the county was overrun by Conservative heelers of all sorts. We found their tracks in the snowbanks, everywhere over the county, there was another gentleman by the name of Francois LeMarchand who figured in that election. I am told he was one of the

Dominion of Canada,
Province of Nova Scotia,
County of Guysborough.

I,	D. P. Floyd, of Guysborough, in the county of Guysborough, barrister, do solemnly declare that :
1.	I board at Grant's Hotel at Guysborough, Nova Scotia.
2.	Between the 24th and 31st day of April, 1904, while in the smoking room or office of said hotel at Guysborough aforesaid, a young man, who had been pointed out to me previously as Francois Le Marchand, entered and engaged me in conversation.
3.	He represented himself as the agent for the Halifax 'Herald' and 'Mail,' and announced his intention of getting the said ' Mail ' into as many homes as possible in Guysborough county. He asked me to subscribe and I, not stating to what party I belonged, refused on the ground that the editorials were of a very low order of merit and intimated that I regretted this very much. In this view he concurred.
4.	Growing confidential he stated that he not only had the ' Mail ' to use for election purposes, but that he had nineteen thousand dollars to spend in the county of Gyusborough, or as he expressed it, ' to place ' in the county before the next election, and that it must be placed to proper advantage. I then remarked ' You must have spent considerable at the recent election. In view of the fact that it did not do the work intended, it is strange that you are going to expend more.' He replied, ' The trouble was that the money did not get into the proper hands. Certain men got it and used it injudiciously. Look at the result at White Head ? Had I control of the funds in other districts I could accomplish the same results.' I said, * There must have been a great deal of money used in purchasing votes at the recent election.' ' How much do you suppose,' he asked. I replied ' about fifteen thousand.' ' More than that,' he said, ' there was twenty-seven thousand dollars spent by the Conservatives in the late election in this county. preparing an article from Guysborough county for tbe ' Herald ' and ' Mail,' but did not say that he was writing over the pen name 1 Oculus.'

Now, Sir, I am informed, although I do not know anything personally about this, that it takes about 100 flasks of whisky to fill a barrel. Mr. Giffin ou that occasion got 65 votes at Mulgrave. The Conservative party must have given to each voter about one and a half flasks of whisky if that calculation is correct. The Conservative candidate got over 1,600 votes in that election and if they treated them all with the same liberality with which they treated the people of Mulgrave they must have supplied about 2,500 flasks of whisky on that occasion. Still the editor of the Truro ' Sun ' turns up the whites of his eyes and talks about the Grits getting votes by the whisky method.
There was another charge made against certain people in Guysborough in reference to decimating the electoral lists to which I think I may be permitted to refer for a few moments as it lias become current throughout Canada in the Conservative papers, l will not refer to it if hon. gentlemen opposite object to me doing so. I did intend on a former occasion to take the opportunity of saying something about that question which has been very persistently discussed throughout the Conservative press and by the Liberal press too. As far as I can discover, the charges are without foundation. The charges were made by an anonymous correspondent in the Halifax ' Herald1 signing himself ' Oculus.' He gave what appeared to he a great number of facts regarding a number of names which he said had been struck from the electoral list of the district of St. Mary's. This was published also with black headlines in the Montreal ' Star,' and a great many editorials have been written in regard to it. The c-harge was also published in the Toronto ' Mail.' While I do not wish to weary the House by reading the letter of ' Oculus,' I may be permitted to read to the committee an abstract of it taken from the Toronto * Mail.' The ' Mail ' says :

The riding consists of two municipalities, one of which is known as St. Mary's. In the recent by-election St. Mary's increased its Liberal majority by 77, although a smaller vote was polled. That at the revision of electoral lists March 5th, A.D. 1904, there were present the revisers, C. W. Pye representing the Liberals and Newman H. McDonald and H. F. Harding in support of other applications. That out of the lists of eighty-two names cited by ' Oculus ' as disfranchised and referred to above, only fourteen applications to add to the electoral lists for A.D, 1904, were made by the Conservatives, the owners of thirty-nine of those names are alive and in this county, without the Conservatives making any effort to secure them the franchise. That as touching the pronounced Conservative leanings of those on the lists cited by ' Oculus ' in the Halifax ' Herald ' as before referred to, in the polling districts of Sherbrooke and Sonora, the Liberals added sixteen names from those lists of, ' Oculus,' the Conservatives only four, their total applications being six, and two they were unable to qualify. That as far as my knowledge goes, intentional wrong by the revisers in this revisal section No. 1 was never intended or committed. I have the fullest confidence in the integrity of my associate revisers, Messrs. Pye and Reid, and I firmly believe that did not their absence from the county, preclude them from making a careful review of the necessary document, they would be pleased to join with me in every part of this declaration, or to make independent declarations of the same tenor, covering their term of office.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously, believing it to be true, and knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act, 1893.
Declared before me at the town of Sherbrooke, in the countfy of Guysborough, this 26th day of May, A.D. 1904.

I would be very pleased to put the answer on record if it is the only answer the Conservatives can make. But let me say that in the first place it is an anonymous answer, and no person has had the courage to make a statement at all over his own signature in regard to this. Now Sir, the only person who did attempt to make any change in the electoral lists in the constituency on that occasion, was Chas. E. Tanner the Conservative organizer in Nova Scotia.
Mr. Tanner approached the returning officer, who is a layman, not a lawyer, and made an application for the addition of certain Conservative names to the electoral list a few days before the election and he attempted to insist on these names being added, saying that there was legal authority for doing so. He got the returning officer into a good deal of confusion but the returning officer refused and very properly refused to add any name to the official list sent him on which the election was to be conducted. This was .the oply attempt made to tamper with the list in the county of Guysborough during that election. It was a bold and impudent attempt to tamper with the lists and was prevented by the refusal of the returning officer to do what was asked by Mr. Tanner. On the strength of these so called revelations, which are not signed by anybody and for whom no person will become responsible, we have been read a great many lectures by the Conservative papers in Canada in which we are told that it is of the first importance that there should be no interference with the lists. I wish to place myself on record as agreeing with that principle, that it is of the utmost
6^85

importance to the people of this country that no man should be allowed to tamper with the ballots and that there should be a fair revision of the lists on [DOT] every occasion. X can assure hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House who do not belong to Nova Scotia and who may have ireadi some of these articles in the Conservative papers throughout Canada in regard to the manner in which the lists are revised in that province, that we have a fair and just revision of the lists and that there is no real reason to complain. I know that we have men on both sides who will try to take advantage of their oppenents and to get their own men on the list and keep the others off. But we have every safeguard around the franchise in Nova Scotia and no man need complain who takes interest enough in, his own affairs to see that his name is recorded. I know of only one case in the history of this country when this right, which every Canadian holds dear was in danger and that was the occasion of the introduction by the predecessors of hon. gentlemen opposite of that precious piece of legislation known as the Dominion Franchise Act. That Act threw the whole question of revising the lists into the hands of partisan revising barristers. These were the only people who had the right to decide whether a man should vote or not vote. That system was created and maintained for the purpose of loading the dice; it was one of the greatest outrages ever perpetrated on a free people and the political party which is responsible for the Dominion Franchise Act and for the Act by which the counties of Ontario were gerrymandered should not find any fault with the Franchise Act of Nova Scotia.

That was the position of affairs during that period. I know that hon. gentlemen opposite have said over and over again that *hey
are not responsible for what their predecessors did and I do not hold them responsible in the same sense, that I hold them responsible for the things which they do themselves. At the same time they are con-, stantly reminding us of the achievements of (their party in the past and it is only right and fair that they should be kept in a humble, lowly and penitent state of mind by being occasionally reminded of the depths of depravity to which their party sank during the pei'iod in which they had the power to control the franchise of the people of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I shall not detain the House very long in replying to the remarks of my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. (Sinclair). I have no doubt that he has had this upon his stomach, so to speak, for some time, and it is therefore only fair that the House should have patience and allow him to get rid of it. I was careful in introducing the subject to the committee to make as little reference as possible to the Guysborough election, because I do not approve of discussing provincial matters in the House. I therefore introduced the subject at the proper time, during the criticism of the estimates of the Minister of Railways and called attention to the action of some officials with the least possible reference to the Guysborough election. Without any reference at all to reports and rumours, I based what I had to say on what I believed to be authentic information and invited the minister to give us the opportunity, by the appointment of a commissioner, to prove the truth of what I have stated. My hon. friend has gone very far afield. He has developed to a large extent the party view of the recent election in Guysborough and he has filled me with pride in the opposition by informing us that that party had at its control in this election large sums of money. I knew that we had virtue. I knew that we had industry and a good cause, but I did not know that we had the money. If my hon. friend had devoted his time to telling what he knew, instead of what he did not know, he could have given us some very valuable information indeed. He could have told us the course of certain cheques that were cashed at banking agencies in Halifax just about that time and which possibly found their way in the course of time to Guysborough.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I could not, Mr. Chairman. I am not aware that any cheques at all were cashed on that occasion relating to my election.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.

I accept the hon. gentleman's statement. I presume my hon. friend was prudent enough to take care not to know much about it. Possibly, however, some other people know a little more. The hon. gentleman has entertained the House with

his revelations as to the crimes and the crookedness of the Conservative party during that election ; and if I ever heard anything absolutely farcical it was the unfolding of his evidence on that point. Anythibg more grotesque and absolutely ridiculous, was never given in the hearing of this House. It was absolutely 1 vox, et praeterea nihil.' There is nothing to it, just rumours and suspicions. He has spoken of certain men named Switzer and Twiger. A man must have a name and there has been no evidence to show that the men did not give their own names.

speechtext:
I do not know how far these assertions that these gentlemen were travelling under incorrect names are true. I recall, however, one matter which was ventilated in this House in which case no less a gentleman than the father of the Solicitor General of this parliament was proved to have made his appearance, during an election in the Magdalen Islauds and there to have represented his distinguished son under an assumed name. He was Mr. Le-mieux when he went to the Magdalen Islands, but in the stimulating air of that district his name grew to Lamirande in the course of a night, Why should not other people have the privilege also of travelling incognito?
The funniest thing of all was that the hon. gentleman has succeeded-and I regret to say in connection with my own country- in disinterring the gentleman who must forever pass as the ehiefest of all the suckers in this world of ours, who met a gentleman called by my hon. friend Francois Le Marchand, who informed this gullible gentleman that he had $27,000 to spend on the last election. I regret very much that Mr. Floyd's habitat has been established in Nova Scotia, for I would like the people to believe that we are not altogether simpletons in that county down by the sea. No man has ever taken the trouble to prove by affidavit that he has been made a fool of to such an extent as our friend Mr. Floyd. Then we had a long statement from Mr. E. M. Macdonald, which contains absolutely nothing whatever. If he does not prove himself better at running elections than at drawing affidavits, it wiil take him some time to get hold of the county

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
of Pictou ; and if he does not know more about running elections in the county of Pictou than he has shown he does in the county of Guysborough, he cannot be very dangerous, and I need not feel much alarmed. But why did the hon. gentleman not give the names of those who found their way into the county of Guysborough in his own interests ? He mentioned three or four who had gone there to represent the Conservative party, and said that the snow banks were covered with their tracks. But a gentleman who was recently his legal partner in New Glasgow was there, and there was no mark of his tracks on any of the snow banks. He had a much more comfortable means of conveyance. He was driven through the county by the gentleman who was deputy returning officer. The deputy returning officer drove my hon. friend's iate law partner, and he carried a very suggestive looking little satchel, of which he took great care. I did not hear that Mr. Patterson addressed any public meeting, but he and his friend the sheriff did drive from house to house, and never parted company with that precious little satchel. I am willing to assume that my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) did not know anything about money in this election. I am willing to assume that it was a perfectly purely conducted election, although there were some surprising turns over in the vote. But when he undertakes to read the Conservative party a lecture on the use of liquor, I think he must have braced himself up with some kind of a bracer-possibly something of the kind that was used plentifully in that campaign. It is not possible that he was altogether ignorant of the fact that a good deal of spirit was thrown into the operation of the Liberal party on that occasion by the old custom of putting spirits down to keep their spirits up. There was a good deal of that sort of thing done, and I am much pleased to find that he regrets that that ancient and time-honoured custom was ever followed. The hon. gentleman made some comments reflecting on a gentleman named Mr. McNab, of Montreal. I am glad, however, that he showed more caution in his strictures than was displayed by the writers of certain articles in the Nova Scotia press. Mr. McNab is a clever and estimable gentleman, who has been undeservedly treated with a great deal of undeserved ignominy by the press of hon. gentlemen opposite. The articles written concerning him were not signed for most excellent reasons, but I regret very much for the fair fame of our province that a gentleman could not go into the neighbourhood of the county of Guysborough, when an election was about to take place, without being treated with such foul abuse as was heaped on Mr. McNab. As an instance of the extremes to wlficli the partisans of hon. gentlemen opposite went, I might men-

tion that one of them in my own county expressed the great regret he felt that Mr. Mc-Nab had not broken his wretched neck on his way home. I might say that Mr. McNab was never in Guysborough. He was in the town of New Glasgow, where I saw him, and certainly there was nothing improper in his conduct^in that town. He was there acting as any gentleman might whose business bad brought him to that place. Why does the hon. gentleman single out this gentleman and not mention any of the other estimable men who were in the county at that time ? Why did he not mention Mr. Kirk, who left the Dorchester penitentiary and went all the way to Guysborough. and spent there a long winter day, from eight in the morning until five o'clock in the evening, in the vicinity of the polls ? Why did he not mention also my friend Mr. Dickie, who was there in the interests of the party opposite, and who had not even a vote in that county, as far as I know, or any particular business apart from politics ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman did not notice that Mr. Kirk said he was only there three or four hours.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
I have credible information to the effect that he was there all day, and I am not disposed to quarrel with my information, which comes from two or three different sources. He did spend many hours in an open sleigh in the immediate vicinity of the polling place. Was he there acting as guard over some of the whisky which was used there in the interests of my hon. friend ? Then, again, the premier of Nova Scotia was there, and also Mr. Macdonald, of the county of Pictou. and Mr. Patterson and a host of others. Why were they not singled out by the hon. gentleman for comment ? But I would ask what is there to prevent anybody from going into that county if he should take an active interest _ in any election there ? No one would question on* this side the right of any citizen to take part in an election, who is free to do so. Why, then, should my hon. friend spend so much of our valuable time in telling us that certain gentlemen had gone into that county to take part in an election ? Surely that is the most natural thing to do. Not long ago I had the pleasure of meeting my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in a county in which he does not live, and I expect td meet him again in several counties in Nova Scotia during the next campaign. It is a part of the duty of public men to take part in an election campaign. If our hon. friend had taken up our valuable time in telling us what he does know, we might derive some benefit from his remarks, "but all he did was discuss things of which he has not any personal-knowledge. - All he did was to indulge in a mass of surmises which were absurd on their face, and he demonstrated their absurdity by this affidavit of Mr. Floyd. If anything would show that the hon. gentleman was not fit to represent a constituency in that province, it is the fact that he seriously discussed such an absurd affidavit, and indulged in such ridiculous surmises. My hon. friend went into the question of the electoral lists, but why deal with that question here ? That question has been thoroughly discussed in the public press. I was in the county myself, and I know that in the St. Mary's district, where I was working, some eighty names were not on the list which should have been there, and this was due to the fact that in that municipality the lists are prepared by revisers appointed by the county council, and that county council is composed of some five or six Liberals and not one Conservative. And in that district there has not yet been appointed one reviser or assessor within the memory of man who is not a partisan of hon. gentlemen opposite. Although these men have to perform judicial duties, they are, without exception, selected from the ranks of the party opposite. Every member of the council is a Grit, and every appointment made, if it has attached to it a salary of 25 cents, is made from the ranks of the Grit party.	.	,
Every electoral list prepared in that county is prepared by these men, and my hon. friend knows as well as I do that some of them are not over-scrupulous. He read an affidavit from a gentleman named Ross, who says, for the purpose of misleading the public outside the county of Guysborough, that one of the men left off the list was an escaped criminal. What are the facts ?
John Bjard did not leave Sherbrooke until after the 1903 revision. He had been on, and there was no change in his circumstances, yet he was struck off. In the spring of 1903, after the revision, he was convicted under the Scott Act of having paid for and passed over to another man one bottle of liquor. That is the criminal warrant. A conviction under the Scott Act is known to be no disqualification under the Scott Act.
Here is a man whose affidavit is read in this House, a man who puts what is practically a lie in his affidavit in order to mislead persons in other portions of Canada who do not know the facts. I need not, after that sample, pursue my inquiries on the character of the Ross affidavit. In the neighbourhood in which he has lived there is no occasion to do so for he is too well known. I could deal with other points in this affidavit, but it is not necessary. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair) could not close without a fling at the Dominion Franchise Act. And yet the government which he supports and on whose behalf he pounds his desk so vigourously themselves proposed to pass a Franchise Act with regard to one province because they have lost tempor-rarily control of the government of that pro-

yinee. But they were compelled to drop the bone they thought to carry away. They may hope, In a short time to recover control, bnt they could not afford to wait. They were quite willing to fly in the face of the principle which they themselves had so often declared for by taking the control of the lists out of provincial hands. The moment a province gets out of their control they are ready to enact for it the law that they denounced so generally and so loudly. The hon. gentleman was not over ingenuous in what he gaid about the Franchise Act. He said that it was passed to enable the former government to appoint partisan revising officers. He spoke of this as being for the whole of Canada-he mentioned two hundred counties, and, though he was not quite right as to the number, it is evident that he had the whole of Canada in mind. He said that the late Conservative government had imposed upon Canada electoral lists made up by partisan barristers. His reputation for strict adherence to facts will not rise very rapidly in this House if he continues to make such statements. He was compelled to acknowledge his error. Being a practising barrister in his own province he could hardly have failed to know that in many of the counties in Nova Scotia, the revising officers were the judges, and in Ontario, it was almost the rule to have the county court judges perform this function. To my mind it would have been, better if the hon. gentleman had not made his speech. He will not add much to his reputation for judgment and sincerity by such speeches, and he has not added much to the esteem in which the people of his county will be held when he produces and reads such absurd affidavits as those to which he has treated the House to-day. He read the statement of Mr. MacDonald which, I think, the House will agree was a ridiculous statement. He might have done better if that hon. gentleman-I do not know that I should say ' honourable ' for it seems a misuse of the term to use it in that connection had prepared his list of voters, Mr. MacDonald was on trial before the grand jury of my county for presenting to the _ sheriff, who was revising officer, affidavits which had been forged and falsified, and he very narrowly escaped spending a portion of his years in a public institution where his keep would not have been at all costly to him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman tell the House the result of that trial 1

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
The result was that the grand jury did not bring in a Bill. There was a friendly judge on the bench and Mr. MacDonald was allowed to go before the grand jury and succeeded in begging off. But there was no question about the facts and he never denied them. If he had brought his talent to bear the hon. gentleman would have had even a better list than that on Mr. BELL.
which he ran and which was a very good one for him, because, to my knowledge, some eighty names were left off the list, and of these almost all were Conservatives. They were not quite all Conservatives-and this will serve to show how nicely this Grit machine works. There were a few Liberals left off. and why ? Because, in a previous municipal election they had ventured to vote for certain men for municipal office who were not acceptable to the Grit machine. That machine cuts off the heads not only of those whom it is not able to control for Dominion elections, but even those who will not obey its behests in municipal elections. ' Altogether my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) might better have left this matter where it should have been left to be discussed-in Guysborough and in Nova Scotia. It is not proper to introduce such subjects in this House. In beginning the few remarks I thought fit to offer I took care to make no reference to my hon. friend. I simply called attention of the Minister of Railways to the fact that certain of his officials were alleged to have taken an active part in elections. My hon. friend has admitted that one government official is president of the Liberal Association of Guysborough. All I wanted to do was to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to the facts and to ask him whether he proposed to apply in these cases the principle laid down by his leader in 1897. When we challenge the conduct of the government in dismissing men for alleged partisanship, the principle was laid down by the right hon. leader of the government that a public official was free to vote as he chose, but was not allowed to take a more active part in political contests. I will watch-and so will others along the line of the Intercolonial- to see whether the Minister of Railways is going to live up to the lofty principle enunciated by his leader. I cannot say I expect very much from him. We can hardly fail to recollect that, when our friends on the other side of the House talk about purity in elections, when they proclaim their love and their devotion, their adoration even, for purity and high principle, it is the same as when certain people talk about honesty- time to button your pockets. We know-it is no matter of hearsay ; it has been proven to a demonstration and is set out broad and clear upon the pages of Canadian history, so that even the most casual reader cannot but note it-that the very things that these gentlemen profess to admire and revere as lofty and pure are the very things that, in practice, they sedulously avoid. They have preached every political virtue and have declared each to be dear to their hearts, but in the practice of these virtues they have been sad failures indeed. If ever a party was branded and stigmatized as being made up of hypocrites, of men wanting in sincerity, that party is the Liberal party of Canada.
At six o'clock, House took recess.

speechtext:
House in committee on Bill (No. 80) respecting the West Canadian Collieries, Limited.-Mr. Oliver.
On the preamble.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: This is a Bill of considerable importance, and I do not think it is properly understood. I hope the promoter will be able to make a satisfactory explanation of the Bill, and that before it goes through we shall have the assurance of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) or the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) that the matter has been investigated, and that the Bill may be passed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: The Bill was up for consideration the week before last, and on the joint suggestion of the leader of the opposition and the Minister of Justice, it was held over for consideration by the Justice Department. That consideration has been given. The legal gentlemen acting for the company discussed the Bill with the Department of Justice and made such alterations in it as the officials of the Justice Department suggested. The Bill in that form went before the Private Bills Committee the second time and was agreed to unanimously, and now it comes before the House in Committee for final approval. I am not in a position to discuss the very intricate question that was raised by the leader of the opposition when the Bill was before the House before, but I think it will be agreed that having been dealt with in this way we may fairly consider it as having been put in a satasfactory shape and proper to be accepted by the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I do not think that explanation is quite sufficient to warrant us in passing this Bill. To my mind it is an extraordinary Bill, it seems to ask for powers to do anything and everything. Though I do not * doubt the statement of the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) that the Minister of Justice has looked into this Bill, still I think the Minister of Justice should be here and give an assurance to the committee that he regards the Bill as one that ought to receive the sanction of this House. But so far as I am concerned I do not think it should.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
As for the preamble I think it is in a very much better shape now than it was before. It reads now as follows :
Whereas the West Canadian Collieries, Limited, hereinafter called the company, has by its petition represented that it was incorporated under ' The Companies Act,1 1862 to 1900, of Great Britain, and has been licensed under 61 Vic., chap. 49 (Dominion) to carry on mining operations in the Yukon and Northwest Territories by license dated the 6th October, 1903.
I assume that all that has been proved to the satisfaction of the committee to which the Bill was referred. Then the preamble proceeds as follows :
Whereas the company has filed a duly certified copy of the company's memorandum and articles of association in the office of the Secretary of State of Canada.
The memorandum and articles of the association correspond to the charter of the company as contained in an Act of parliament, and set forth the powers of the company and the purpose for which it was incorporated. The preamble proceeds as follows :
And whereas the company has, by its petition, prayed that it be enacted as hereinafter set forth, and it is expedient to grant the prayer of the said petition.
Of course we have to consider that in connection with what follows, we are on the preamble now. I do not see any objection to the preamble in its present form.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: The trouble with it is that it is an incorporated company under the Joint Stock Companies Act of England from 1862 to 1900, the Act as amended during that time. It comes over here and receives a license under the Land Act, empowering it to carry on mining, or grazing, or timber business. That license is an entirely different thing from an incorporation. Then we unite that license with the letters of incorporation and embody it in an Act of parliament here, leaving in it all the provisions which the original corporation contained. We do not know what the provisions of the Joint Stock. Companies Act were, what powers they have under it, but whatever they are or whatever they were they are renewed here. It seems to me doubtful whether we should pass this Bill. The Minister of Justice above all others ought to be the one to examine it and guide us, otherwise we are practically going it blind.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
I can assure the committee that the Minister of Justice coincided to a great degree with the remarks of the leader of the opposition, and took the responsibility of reviewing the Bill so as to bring it into line with the laws of Canada. I think the committee will remember that I asked him particularly : Do you take the responsibility of doing this, and he said he did. Now he has discharged that responsibility, the Department of Justice has reviewed the Bill, and some changes have been made in it at the request of the Justice Department. The Bill has gone through the Private Bills Committee and so far as the promoters of the Bill are concerned every requirement has been complied with in order to bring it within the rules of the

House and within the general procedure in such cases provided.

speechtext:
Section 1 is struck out and the following inserted :
The company shall he and is hereby recognized throughout the Dominion of Canada as a body corporate and politic by and under the name of the * West Canadian Collieries, Limited,' but such recognition shall not deprive the company of the power to make such variations in its constitution as it may lawfully make in virtue of the Companies Act, 1862 to 1900, and under the statutes of the Imperial parliament in amendment thereof or substitution therefor ; and such recognition shall not be deemed to authorize or empower the company to exercise in the Dominion of Canada any power or to do any act for the lawful exercise or doing of which an Act of the parliament of Canada would otherwise have been necessary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
I would be inclined to think this clause is fairly well guarded now. It has been pointed out that there might be possibly an objection to it. Really there is no very great object in enacting it at all. It practically does not differ from what the law would otherwise be because a company incorporated in a foreign country can in Canada, by virtue of what is known as the comity of nations, carry on its business and is recognized as a corporation internationally by the comity of courtesy of international law. Of course Great Britain has a different legislature from ours although it belongs to the same empire. The same treatment would be given to a company incorporated in a foreign country like the United States, or Germany, or Prance, so that this section does effect very much change. The section as drafted goes on to make this provision :
-and such recognition shall not be deemed to authorize or empower the company to exercise in the Dominion of Canada any power or to do any act for the lawful exercise or doing of which an Act of the parliament of Canada would otherwise have been necessary.
Therefore, the section does not really seem to me to add very much to what the company might otherwise do, and I suppose it is inserted for the reason that as powers are given further on, it is advisable in the first instance to recognize the company formally by statute, although that recognition does not seem to me as a matter of law to carry the company beyond the position in which it would have found itself under the law apart from this statute altogether. It is quite true that power is reserved to the company to make changes under the English Companies Act, 18621900 and to carry on its business in Canada, but it had the right to do that anyway. That is to say that a company incorporated in Great Britain which has a different legislature from our own or in-Mr. OLIVER.
corporated in any foreign country can come to Canada and carry on business, and carrying on business in Canada, it can by virtue of the legislature of this country or under the authority of the legislature of its own country make changes in its constitution or powers and after that, of course, as respects the powers of the company, they are limited by these changes. I do not think there is in the first section anything to which we might reasonably object. There may be a clause further on where very extensive powers are given the company to which some valid objection might be made, but as far as this section is concerned, I do not think there is any objection to be made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: What position would we be in suppose we wanted to wind up the company ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: That depends on a careful examination of the Winding Up Act, but I imagine the company would have to be wound up in Great Britain where its head office is. The courts in Canada would be auxiliary to the courts of Great Britain for that purpose, and we would have the right in this country to see that the assets were so applied that no injustice would be done to Canadian creditors.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I have had little experience in dealing with a foreign company, and that very troublesome question came up. How should the company be wound up 1 You have in the Winding Up Act a provision which sets out how the assets of the company shall be used for the liquidation of its liabilities, but there may be obligations resting upon the company in a foreign country and the question arose as to how the assets should be used. There was a conflict of jurisdiction. What authority would we have to deal with a foreign corporation and use the assets to satisfy the Canadian creditors, while the English creditors, or in the case that I have referred to. the American creditors, would not be satisfied ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
A difficult and important question arises in regard to that. I am not prepared to say that the company might not be wound up in this country.' I will not say anything about that at the present moment without investigating the statutes. In cases where companies incorporated in Great Britain have become insolvent while carrying on business in this country the question has sometimes arisen-it has arisen in my own province-whether liens obtained under the law of the province should prevail against the title of the trustee in Great Britain. In my own province we have held that liens granted under the law of our own province should take precedence of the title of the trustee. I do not know whether

the same would apply to other provinces. At all events the Canadian creditors would stand in the same position as the creditors in Great Britain. Their rights would be respected, they could tile their claims and participate in the assets just in the same same way as the English creditors would. Of course, as far as the winding up of the company is concerned, there would be exactly the same difficulty if this company were not coming to this parliament for its Act of incorporation at all. The company might carry on business in this country without coming to this parliament under the doctrine that I have already mentioned, it might become insolvent and if it had to be wound up, the same difficulties* to which my hon. friend has referred would arise in that case.
On section 4, subsection (n).

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I think it is hardly worth while striking out any of these words because I think that nearly every power that could be given to the company is given. I hardly think it worth while striking out a few words. I think we ought to have some members of the administration here to say that this is a proper Bill, that it has been investigated and examined and that the government is prepared to say that it has the approval of the departmental officers under whose notice it should come;, because, to my mind, it is one of those sweeping, blanket charters that covers almost everything. and it will be a very strange matter indeed if it does not come in contact with private interests that we cannot detect from a cursory reading of the Bill.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I am very sorry that the hon. member foiv Halton (Mr. Henderson) should take the position which he does. I beg to assure him that the Department of Justice has reviewed the Bill, that the amendments contained are amendments suggested by the department and agreed to by the parties promoting the Bill. There cannot be anything more evident than that, by the very fact that the amendments which have been read have conformed to the suggestions then made by the leader of the opposition, and agreed to at that time, measurably at any rate, by the Minister of Justice. The whole of the amendments and the whole of the procedure has been in the last degree regular, and I would think it is hardly fair for the hon. member to practically say that my word in this matter is not good. I beg to assure the House that it is.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
I have stated that I was quite prepared to take the hon. gentleman's word, but it may be within the recollection of us all that not very long ago he read a very severe lecture to members on this side of the House for being absent when business came before the House. I objected to this Bill when it was last called
simply because the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) was absent, and I thought as he was so extremely particular that every hon. member on this side of the House should be in his place, that it was just as well that his Bill should stand over. I notice that neither the Minister of Justice nor the Minister of the Interior is present to-night, and surely one of these ministers should be here to vouch for the propriety of this Bill. . Considering the strong position which the promoter of this Bill has taken with regard to members not being in their places when matters of this kind came up, I am disposed to follow his example and to insist that the proper minister be here to vouch for this legislation. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) chooses to read lectures to this side of the House, then when an opportunity occurs we have a perfect right to read a lecture back to him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: Are the powers enumerated in section 4 in conformity with those contained in the memorandum or articles of association of the company. I would presume they are, but it is Important that we should have some assurance as to that. Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) know ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I am not in a position to answer the question. I repeat that the Private Bills Committee considered the Bill and reported unanimously in favour of it in its present shape. That is the only assurance I can give the committee on the subject.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
In England there is practically no restriction to the powers they give to these companies and possibly the provisions of section 4 have simply been copied from the memorandum or article of association of the company as it is now constituted in which case there might be no very great objection to it.
Section agreed to on division.
On section 5,

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
Section 5 seems to give this company extraordinary power. Could it come into the county which I have the honour to represent and erect telegraph and telephone poles through the villages without any restriction whatever. Surely the hon. member (Mr. Oliver) should imagine that the people of this country have some rights. I take no exception because this is an English company ; I am very glad indeed that they are investing capital here to develop the country, but I think there should be some restriction so that we can actually say that we have a little claim upon our own property and some right to go out and in. If it were a Canadian company these restrictions would be placed around it. I can hardly believe for one moment that the Minister of Justice has assented to this Bill, and I must protest against its proceeding to-

night until we have some further assurance. I move that the committee rise, report pro-gresss, and ask leave to sit again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: The practice is that all these Bills are dealt with by committees representing the House, and I presume that the committee has inquired into this Bill and given it due consideration. I am not a member of the committee, but I accept the statement of the bon. member (Mr. Oliver) that the Minister of Justice has advised on this Bill, and if so, I presume that he has passsed on this section because there is some provision in the genera! Act which will protect the municipalities with regard to telephone and telegraph poles. I do not imagine that the Minister of Justice would permit a Bill to go through for the purpose of allowing a company to take possession of the streets of any municipality, and I am bound to believe that there must be some governing provision in the general Act. I am not familiar with the Bill and I cannot say that the Minister of Justice has given attention to all these things but I think it is a fair presumption. If there is any grave objection to the Bill I have no desire to see it pressed to-night.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: There may be something in the statement of the minister, but I think further there is no provision in the Bill enabling it to enter upon public highways. As to constructing conduits : that is made subject to the consent of the municipalities. The power to construct telegraph and telegraph lines won!4 not imply power to enter upon the streets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: Nor on private land without compensation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I do not think there would be much danger so far as that is concerned, but as to conduits I think the limitations in clause 4 are not quite adequate. There are districts in the Northwest Territories which have no municipal government and the provision as to municipal control would not have very much application. I should think it would be in the interests of the constituents of my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) that there should be some further restriction in the Bill as to that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: If I were understood as saying that the Minister of Justice bad personally overlooked this Bill, I did not wish to say so. I say that I'lie officers of his department did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: That is what I understood.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
And so, I suppose the Minister of Justice would be practically responsible for the amendments that have been made. I think that the point which the leader of the opposition has suggested is well taken. Where there are no municipalities that difficulty, however, could be cured very easily by providing that in such Mr. HENDERSON.
cases the government of the Northwest Territories, who really control all highways, should have the power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: We might insert the words ' or other authority.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I think it would be proper to put in such words as are necessary to make the amendment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
I may say that this Bill has not been before the Railway Committee at all. I find that under this particular clause -the company are taking power to
Construct, operate and dispose of telegraph and telephone lines for the purpose of its [DOT]undertakings only.
Of course, the words giving the company power to do this for its own purposes form just the usual clause which is put in all Bills, but I think before a matter of this kind is passed in this committee it should be referred to the Railway Committee, which is accustomed to dealing with questions of this kind and which imposes certain safeguards. I also notice in clause 6 :
The company may, for the purpose of any of its undertakings or for the promotion thereof, construct) and operate all such railway sidings, tramways, switches or spur lines, not exceeding ten miles in length, as are necessary to connect the works and properties of the company with each other or with the line of any railway company incorporated by or under the control of parliament.
That is a matter which seems to me to be directly under the power of the Railway Committee. My attention hits just been called to these provisions in the Bill, and I think that under the circumstances it should be referred back to the Railway Committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I supposed it had gone to the Railway Committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I am explaining that it has not gone to the Railway Committee ; it went to the Private Bills Committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I should think it ought to have gone to the Railway Committee.	[DOT]

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I would move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. In the meantime the Bill should be referred to the Railway Committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
This matter was fully considered by the Private Bills Committee. This company was an English company incorporated under the laws of England. We in Canada were simply trying to give them the powers which they already had under their English charter, so far as they were consistent with Canadian law. No power of expropriation, as I remember, is granted, They would only have the power to construct a line not to exceed ten miles in length, a spur line for the purposes of their

own business, and the telegraph and telephone lines were on the same basis.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: If they are given the powers suggested by the hon. gentleman, then, under the General Railway Act, they will be able to construct their road upon a public highway if they get the consent of the Railway Commission. It is not the policy of the Railway Committee to allow railways to run on highways without the con sent of the municipalities, and that is another reason why it should go to the Railway Committee. I have no doubt that is what was in the mind of the chairman ot the Railway Committee (Mr. Hyman) when he asked to have this referred to the Railway Committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: We do not apply the Railway Act, and there can be no power to enter on highways under this Bill.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I do not desire to enter upon the merits but certainly clauses 5 and 6 refer to telephones and railways, and that being the case, the Bill ought to be considered by the Railway Committee before it is submitted to the. House. That is my only reason for making this motion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I would like to point out to the committee that the question raised by the acting Minister of Public Works and Chairman of the Railway Committee (Mr. Hyman) was thoroughly considered by the parties who are promoting the Bill ; and as their enterprise is entirely a private one, and as they ask for no powers of a public character, they did not consider that it came under the jurisdiction of the Railway Committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: How does the hon. gentleman think that they could obtain the power to build ten miles of railway to connect their works with any line of railway incorporated by this parliament without coming before the Railway Committee ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I suppose they would connect just as any other railway would connect or just as any crossing would be made over any other railway, and that would be by obtaining the consent of the Railway Commission. This Bill does not ask for authority to construct a telegraph or telephone or railway line as a public enterprise, but only to construct such for the purposes of operating their coal mines and coak ovens.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: What is the difference?

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: There is all the difference in the world.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
Why should they not
have that power ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
Why not ? These people are operating coal mines on a very large scale and also coke ovens. Is this parliament going to say to them : you shall not put up a telephone line between your two
sets of coke ovens or coal mines. Or you shall not connect them by a railway ? They are a coal mining company, and they happen to be located some five or six miles distant from the Crow's Nest Pass branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and in order to get their output to market, they must reach that railway by a railway line. They have a railway line from their present coal mines to the Crow's Nest branch under a railway charter, which comes under the Railway Act, and is a public enterprise. They have also other coal mines in other places which are not yet developed, but to which they are prepared to build other railway lines, also secured under charter from this parliament. Where they are building a railway line as a public enterprise, they come under the provisions of the Railway Act, but where they want to lay down a pair of rails for the transport of their own output, they are not asking to be put under the Railway Act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: Is that mentioned in their charter ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: Half the railway charters that come before the Railway Committee contain a list of powers given by the committee which are not connected with railroading at all. This company is asking to be empowered to do certain things but not to be empowered to do them over the heads of other people. That is the difference between the two conditions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman would admit that if this company asks for power to do a certain thing, we have the right to say on what terms arwl conditions to sanction the doing of certain things, and this parliament has the light to determine on what conditions they shall be done, and as this is a matter concerning telegraphs, telephones and railway lines, the acting minister is perfectly right in saying that it should come before the Railway Committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: This discussion is now out of order. The only motion before the Chair is that the committee rise and report.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: That is in connection with the end of clause 5.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: I am trying very hard to show that the motion should not be agreed to. I submit that the question is a general one and must receive a general answer. In reply to the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), the difference is between asking for a privilege and a power.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman seriously argue that when the company asks a privilege this House should not say on what terms that privilege would be granted ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: Undoubtedly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: Then if it is a question of a railway, surely he will see that it is the Railway Committee which should deal with it. And the very fact that the hon. member promoting the Bill wants to avoid the Railway Committee may cause members to think that this charter is one that should be scrutinized by that committee. I think he had better accept the suggestion of the acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) and have the matter discussed on its merits in that committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
I would be the last man in this House to deny the authority of the House to do as it pleases. Parliament is supreme ; it can take away to-day rights that it gave yesterday. I am not arguing against this Bill going before the Railway Committee, but I am arguing against the idea that those who promoted the Bill did not know what they were doing or that they tried to avoid going before the Railway Committee.
Mr. hi MAN. It is not the promoter of the Bill who sends it to the Railway Committee. The promoter comes before the House and asks for certain privileges, and the House l'efers the matter to the committee that it thinks has jurisdiction.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: But the point I wish to make is that this Bill, according to good legal authority does not need, under the rules of the House, to go to the Railway Committee, inasmuch as it deals with a private and not with a public enterprise. At the same time, if the House says that it must go before the Railway Committee, certainly there is no objection whatever. But there is every objection to the idea being put forward, as was suggested by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) a few moments ago, and as was the logical outcome of the suggestion of the acting Minr ister of Public Works, that, iu the nature of things, it should have gone to the Railway Committee, for we say that in the nature of the case it should not have gone to the Railway Committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: It seems to me that the proposition of the acting Minister of Public Works is the proper one, if the Bill stands in the form in which it was printed. Section 13 expressly provides that section 195 of the Railway Act, 1903, shall apply to the powers given to the company by paragraph (M) of section 4 of the Bill. Paragraph (M) of the Bill deals with electric powers. And, turning to section 195 you will find many provisions there about municipalities and other matters that ought to be considered by the committee that deals with Railways and Telegraphs.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
In reference to section 6, I think the contention of the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) is correct. This Mr. OLIVER.
only empowers the company to construct and operate such railway sidings, tramways, switches or spur lines not exceeding ten miles in length, as are necessary to connect the works and properties of the company with each other'or with any line of railway. I doubt if it gives them power to pass over even a municipal road without the authority of the municipality or of the local legislature of the territories.
Mr, BARKER. But section 195 of the Railway Act expressly applies to lines and wires on the highway, and that section is the one that is applied by section 13 of the Bill.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: Further than that, though this Bill may appily only to a railway on the company's own land, there are some provisions of the Railway Act which it might be necessary to call into operation in connection with the work, as, for example, the provisions with regard to the safety of employees and with regard to the safety of the public, especially in the prevention of fires.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext:
I have no objection.
Progress reported.

maintopic: SUPPLY-LETTER OF MR. W. T. R.
speechtext: With the consent of the House, I beg to move that Bill (No; 80) rest-pecting the West Canadian Collieries, Limited, be referred to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: Before we dispose of that item, I want to refer to one statement that was made by the member for Guys-borougb (Mr. Sinclair). It is proper that I should do so, because of what I call ms wholesale slander of the judges, especially those of Ontario. He stated that over 200 partisan revising barristers dealt with the old Franchise Act, and it was desired to do away with them. Now, there are 213 constituencies in Canada, and if there was a revising barrister for each one there would be 213 of them. In Ontario there are 92 constituencies, and if there were one revising barrister for each there would be 92 ot them. In these 92 I am within the mark in saying that there were not 16 revising bai-risters in the province of Ontario outside the judges: most of the ordinary judges are doing that work to-day. That is an attacl^ upon the judges that was unwarrantable, unjustifiable, and which comes with, bad grace from a prominent lawyer. It seems to be only a bit of the parrot-like talk that has been indulged in by his friends without any proper justification. I wish to resent on behalf of the judiciary of the country this slander on men who are doing the same work they did for many years. In my riding there are three constituencies and only two judges, and you are obliged to appoint one revising barrister besides these two judges. The law required that the party appointed must be a barrister of five years' standing, because only a barrister of five years' standing was eligible to be appointed a judge. The barrister who did that work for years is now the judge of the county and has been for many years. All over the country the provincial lists where they are used to-day are revised by the very same men. They were judges of the county court then and they are judges to ckay ;' and I have not yet heard, in my part of'the country at least, any insinuation by Conservative or Reformer that when they went before these judges or revising barristers they did not get fair-play or were not satisfied.
