speechtext:
I would also like to say a few words with regard to the observations of the member for Guysborougli (Mr. Sinclair). He took occasion to refer to some gentlemen in the province of Nova Scotia whom I know very well, and charac-erized them as heelers. The gentlemen whom he named were Mr. Ernest Gregory, with whom I am very well acquainted, Mr. Charles E. Tanner and Mr. Simpson. I do not recollect any other names. I understood him to designate these gentlemen as heelers, if I understood him correctly. I can only say to my bon. friend and to the House that these are very respectable men
in the province of Nova Scotia, and I think they will bear comparison with my hon. friend in point of reputation and ability.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: I do not think I used that word with regard to these gentlemen who are named. I did have occasion to speak of certain Conservatives, but I did not have these gentlemen in my mind at the time I used that expression. I do not think that what I said would bear the meaning the leader of the opposition seems to have put upon it. At all events, I did not intend that.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext:
I am very glad my hon. friend did not intend it. I do not see that his words could bear any other construction, because these were the gentlemen he named as having been in the county, and afterwards he referred to Conservative heelers in the county. He referred to some one else, but he did not name the other gentlemen to whom he referred. So far as these gentlemen are concerned, all of them whom I have named-I do not know what Mr. Simpson he refers to, but I do know Mr. Tanner and I know Mr. Gregory-they are accustomed to take an important part in the pub lie life of the province. This was not the first occasion on which they have gone into counties where elections were in progress, and I suppose it is not the first occasion on which my hon. friend has gone into counties . where he was not resident when elections were proceeding.
I would also suppose that if my hon. friend desired to make a fair presentation of the irrelevant matter he brought to the attention of the committee, he would not only have read the answer but the letter to which the answer was given, and the reply which was made to that answer. He characterized that answer as absolutely unworthy of notice, and yet one single para graph of it, read by my hon. friend from Fictou (Mr. Bell), absolutely disposed of a very important part of the charge contained in the letter or affidavit of Mr. Ross. In any event, I suppose it would be a fairer course to submit the whole matter to the judgment of the House than to read one side of it.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend allow me to interrupt him ? I would like the hon. gentleman to inform the House who made that answer. I have not yet been able to discover that any reputable person made any reply to Mr. Ross's affidavit, and if the leader of the opposition is able to tell us who it was, I would like very well to have his name.

maintopic: SUPPLY.

I think it is pretty well understood now what the position of the political parties is on the question of patronage and on the question of public servants taking part in elections. The Conservative party, when in power, did not allow government employees to take an offensive part in elections. In 1897 we had the platform laid down by the leaders of the present government to the effect that every employee has a perfect right to vote as he pleases, but if he takes an offensive part in an election he is liable to be dismissed- after an investigation perhaps in some cases. It is well understood among the public servants of Canada that if they take an offensive stand in elections, should the government change hands, the same justice that was meted out to our friends in 1S97 and 1898 will be meted out to them. Therefore, it is well understood, and they know what their position is exactly. But I want to draw the attention of the committee to this further fact. That is all very well as far as the two political parties are concerned, the Conservative, party and the Liberal party, but there is a class of people in this country who are not very strong party men, who care very little about politics, but the question they are concerned in is that if the political parties abuse the power they have by employing a large number of unnecessary men, they are compelled to put their hands in their pockets and pay taxes in order to meet this unnecessary expense. Under these circumstances, they have a right to complain. I hold that in connection with one of the greatest public works that we bave in the Dominion of Canada, namely, 1,500 or 1,600 miles of government railway, it should be no part of any political party's duty to select the men because they are either Grits or Tories who are to be employed on that railway. We have on the floor of this House the manager of the government railway, and if that gentleman were a member of this .House at this moment and were permitted to get up and say whether or not he lias been interfered with ijs general manager of that railway by partisans who are pressing upon him and his officers the employment of unnecessary help, I go so far as to say that he would confirm my statement in that regard. The general manager sent the chief police officer of the railway to Halifax to arrest the men. This officer secured the assistance of the Halifax police, but before the man eauld be secured he had gone.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext:
The minister has given me some information which I did not ask for,
1!

but has not given me the information for which I did ask. I asked him if he could give us an idea of how much of this cost of repairs to engines, passenger cars, postal, express and baggage cars, freight cars and so on was due to accidents and not by wear and tear. That was the question I asked the hon. minister because the expense last year for those purposes was very much greater than the year before. We ought to have some idea of the loss accruing to the country through accidents and in that way 'get a better idea of the management than we could in any other. The minister talks of gentlemen referring to the good roadbed and good service on the Intercolonial. I may say that the last time I came from St. John. I came around by the Intercolonial and have great pleasure in testifying that I think the carriages ran very smoothly and the road appeared to be very good. But 1 thought that we ought to be able to travel a little faster. I think that twenty-three hours from St. John to Montreal is altogether too long. When you go by the Canadian Pacific Railway, you take not half that time.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: There is only half the distance.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: I was glad to find that a new train, was put on which is called the Ocean Express, which is said to do the run in a shorter time. How much shorter ?

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: About three hours.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: It seems to me that this change should have been put in the time table.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: The train did not start until Sunday and it is in the new time table, which is out.	. [DOT]

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: The train started before the time table was out. Would the minister give us a statement of the accidents which have happened on the Intercolonial and the increased expenditure they entailed ? I did not see in any statement of the minister where he procured the money to pay for the accident that happend ter the Canadian Pacific Railway train. Where was that appropriation taken from ? It does not come in under ' Repairs to passenger cars.'

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: The cars were taken to the shops and repaired.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: What about those which were smashed beyond repair ?

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: They were sent to the Canadian Pacific Railway and were paid for by the Intercolonial. That would appear in the general repairs.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: Is that included in the statement you gave us yesterday ?

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: That would appear in the general statement of the whole year.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: Then the statement announced yesterday does not give the full deficit, because it does not include those cars.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: I do not know what the full deficit will be until I get the full returns for June. I am only speaking of the actual payments up to the 31st of May.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: The payments'have already been made for the train belonging to the Canadian Pacific Railway V

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: The general manager says he does not know whether they were paid for or not.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: The item would be quite considerable.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: I think I have said it would be from $25,000 to $35,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: The minister does not know whether that is included in the statement he made ?

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: No, I have not the returns of the Canadian Pacific Railway. AVe sent the cars to the Canadian Pacific Railway. They make the repairs and the Intercolonial is responsible to the Canadian Pacific Railway for the cost.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: I do not think that the public will feel reassured by the statement of the minister with regard to the great length of time which has been allowed to elapse between the accident and the investigation into it. It will be rather depressing to the public to find that an accident can happen and no attempt at an investigation be made until a month later. I certainly would not look upon that as an evidence of good management. I would like to have an assurance from the minister that some sort 6f investigation has been made into the last accident which occurred three or four days ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: An investigation has been held by the officers of the Intercolonial and a further investigation will be held by the inspector, who will take evidence under oath. Parties will be heard under oath before him. The public will be invited to appear and give evidence and the railway officials will also be called upon to testify. Now, as to keeping any account of the cost of cars injured by accident as contradistinguished from the cost of cars that have been worn by use, I may explain that we do not keep a separate account. The only way by which we can get an idea of what accidents cost is through the estimate made at the time of each accident. We know that the accident at Milford will cost at least $30,000 in loss of cars, and there are other expenses besides.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext:
Before the item passes, would the hon. minister inform me if in the statement of receipts and expenditure on

speechtext: FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved the adjournment of the House.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: What business will be taken up to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: The order for supply will be called, and the Minister of Trade: and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) will be the first minister whose estimates will be taken up. If his estimates are disposed of early, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prflfontaine) will probably follow. If not then the Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson).

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: I understood from the Prime Minister privately that some Bills would be taken up in the forenoon of this week, between the time when he spoke to me and Friday. That has been departed from.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: The programme will be as I have stated.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Will the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) be kind enough to bring down the papers in connection with the overrulings in the matter of Corry & Laverdure ? I wrote to the minister some time ago on the subject.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12 o'clock midnight.
Thursday, July 7, 1904.
